meta.title: Should Parcelbird launch its own quick-commerce grocery delivery service in 2027?
meta.subtitle: Assessment of the Parcelbird Now proposal and recommendation to the board · Board meeting, January 2027
meta.purpose: Decide whether to launch Parcelbird Now, a 15-minute grocery delivery service, in 2027
meta.confidentiality: Prepared from the board briefing pack only (synthetic benchmark data); no external research

inputs.label: Finished analysis deck, extracted to text

storyline.governing_thought: Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; invest in the software business, which can reach profitability within current cash

exec_summary.text: The market is growing fast, but no operator makes money in it

sub_points.text: The launch case needs six conditions to hold, and the evidence supports none of them
GMV grew 42% a year in 2022–25, yet both incumbents lose money on every order and one is retreating

exec_summary.text: A dark store would lose money on every order, and customers leave before repaying their acquisition cost

sub_points.text: It loses $6.17 per order at the median and $1.76 at best observed; only a plan beyond any real site profits
Our pop-up lost $12.57 per order, and only 22% of its customers were still ordering in month 3

exec_summary.text: Even on the founders' own numbers, the launch breaks the investors' cash constraints

sub_points.text: It needs $9.5M against $7.2M spendable above the runway floor; with core burn, cash runs out in month 13

exec_summary.text: The software business is a better use of the same cash

sub_points.text: It breaks even in about month 26 at 60% growth and keeps 12 months of runway while growth stays at 34%+

exec_summary.text: Decline the launch, back the software plan with phased hires, and set triggers before any re-entry

sub_points.text: Approve $0.8M a year of hires in tranches, build a store-based offer for grocers, track four triggers

next_steps.action: Decline the 2027 launch of Parcelbird Now and do not extend the pop-up
Release the first tranche of the $0.8M software hires against signed late-stage contracts
Build and test a store-based fast-delivery offer with late-stage pipeline grocers
Set up the quarterly re-entry trigger dashboard and monthly runway reporting
Review conversions, pilot interest and ARR growth against 34%; hold tranche 2 if below

sidebar.header: No combination of observed inputs makes money
bullets: **Best observed:** the best AOV ($42) and the best density (1,400 orders a day) come from different sites; combining them is already optimistic, and it still loses money
**Nine stores:** −$2.0M a store a year means −$18.2M for the median network and −$8.1M at best observed; only the plan's inputs give a profit, +$11.9M
**Break-even AOV:** with other inputs held, the median store needs $63 and the best-observed store $50, against a median of $34 and a best of $42

footnotes: Inputs (AOV, promotions, orders per rider-hour, orders a day): pop-up $31, 12%, 2.1, 280; median $34, 6%, 2.4, 900; best $42, 6%, 3.0, 1,400; plan $45, 2%, 3.5, 1,800
After site fixed cost spreads each store's $1.15M a year of rent, staff and utilities (pop-up $0.65M); both measures exclude HQ overhead, capex and marketing

lead_message.text: The plan must beat the best site observed on all four drivers; median AOV or rider productivity alone turns it loss-making

slides.rationale: One driver at a time set to the median -> bar chart; the stretch beyond observed results reads in the sidebar
slides.unit_line: **Plan contribution per order after site fixed cost, with one driver at the benchmark median**, $ per order

sidebar.header: The plan needs more than the best site on every driver
bullets: **AOV:** $45, 7% above the best site's $42 (median $34); **promotions:** 2% of AOV, 4 percentage points below the best site's 6%
**Riders and density:** 3.5 orders per rider-hour and 1,800 orders a day, 17% and 29% above the top of the observed ranges (1.9–3.0 and 400–1,400)
**Exposure:** at the median, AOV or rider productivity alone turns the plan negative; density or promotions alone leave a thin $0.2–0.3 per order, with nothing for HQ overhead or marketing

footnotes: 9 stores × 1,800 orders a day × $45 × 365 = $266M, about 5% of the 2025 US market; GMV taken as roughly equal to an operator's revenue
slides.so_what: Scale check: nine plan stores would sell $266M a year, more than QuickBasket's $210M revenue

lead_message.text: No evidence yet that we run stores better: our Columbus pop-up trailed the benchmark median on every driver

slides.rationale: Three cases on four drivers against the median -> heatmap with the median as reference row
slides.unit_line: **Profit drivers: Columbus pop-up (six weeks, autumn 2026) against the benchmark median and the founders' plan**

sidebar.header: The pop-up is our only test of a capability edge
bullets: **The claim:** "we know how to run them better than anyone"; the pop-up did worse than the median of the stores our software runs
**Against the median:** AOV 9% lower, promotions twice as high, 13% fewer orders per rider-hour, 69% fewer orders a day
**Fair caveat, it was early:** orders grew 18% a week, from about 178 a day to about 407 in week 6 (our estimate), but with 12% promotions and $38 CAC
sidebar.implication: Ramp-up alone does not close the gap: even at median density the store would still lose $6.17 per order (p. 5)

units.text: Do not launch Parcelbird Now in 2027; invest in the software business, which can reach profitability within current cash
The founders' hypothesis (launch 9 dark stores, contribution-positive by month 18) fails all six conditions it needs
US quick-commerce GMV grew 42% a year 2022–25 (CAGR 41.5%)
Both incumbents lose money on every order: EBITDA margins −26% and −46%, contribution −$1.90 and −$3.40
QuickBasket closed 4 of its 11 cities (36%) in 2025; Zipcart is positive only in its densest city after a fee rise
Growth alone does not justify entry; 'nobody owns the Midwest' may mean nobody has made it pay
At benchmark median a store loses $6.17 per order, $2.67 of it before site cost, so volume cannot fix it
Riders cost $7.40 per order, 81% of goods margin; two of three cities consider minimum pay standards
Best observed on every driver still loses $1.76 per order; only the founders' plan (+$2.02) makes money
Nine stores: −$18.2M a year at median, −$8.1M at best observed, +$11.9M on plan inputs
Break-even AOV is $63 (median) and $50 (best observed) against $34 median and $42 best
The founders' plan needs results beyond the best site ever observed on all four drivers
If AOV or rider productivity is only at the median the plan loses money; density or promotions alone leave about $0.2–0.3 per order
Scale check: plan sales of $266M a year exceed QuickBasket's $210M revenue and are about 5% of the US market
The Columbus pop-up was below the benchmark median on every driver: no evidence of a capability edge
Pop-up caveat: early, temporary site; 18% weekly growth came with 12% promotions and $38 CAC; ramp estimated by constant compounding
Ramp-up alone does not close the gap: at median density the store still loses $6.17 per order
Customers do not stay long enough to repay $38 CAC: 44% stated weekly intent against 22% still ordering in month 3; never repaid at median, 15 months on plan
Zipcart's profitable city needed a $3.99 fee, promotions cut to 1% and lost 14% of volume; the same moves leave our median store at −$1.05
With Zipcart's moves break-even needs about 1,042 orders a day: 16% above median, 3.7 times the pop-up
The launch needs $9.5M against $7.2M spendable above the 12-month runway floor
With today's core burn on top, runway falls below 12 months in month 5 and cash runs out in month 13
All-in reading of the $9.5M leaves $2.5M at month 18, about 6 months of runway; both readings breach the rule
A new funding round for a delivery operator is 'unlikely'; a benchmark 9-store network loses about $1.5M a month
The runway floor rises once stores operate, so the $7.2M headroom is a ceiling
Of options A (launch), B (one pilot store) and C (software-first + store-based fast delivery), only C meets both investor constraints
Option B pilot loses: −$6.17 median economics, ~$2.0M a year loss, runway breached in month 10, little new learning
Cash paths: A runs out in month 13 (low −$2.5M), B drifts to $0.2M, C bottoms at $5.4M then turns cash-positive
Cash model assumptions: burn = opex − gross profit, opex flat apart from $0.8M hires; A capex and $4.1M phasing; B median losses; runway = cash ÷ recurring burn
Software-first breaks even in month 26 at 60% growth (36 at 40%, 41 at 34%), lowest cash $5.4M / $2.7M / $1.2M, runway never below 24 / 18 / 12 months
Software-first holds the runway rule only while ARR grows at least 34% a year; at 25% cash runs out
Break-even ARR = $8.9M ÷ 81% = $11.0M against $4.1M today
Pipeline supports the hires: 9 late-stage grocers worth $0.86M, all 37 worth $3.55M; hires pay for themselves with about 10 contracts (28%)
34% growth means about 15 net new contracts in year 1 (60%: 26); costs flat apart from hires; no churn or win rates, so phase the hires
Risk register: rider pay +20% (+$1.48/+$1.01), density, AOV, competitor, software growth below 34%, cost base, grocers' own fast delivery; most strengthen 'don't launch'
Re-entry triggers: site profit for two quarters; AOV ≥ $42 and ≥ 3.0 orders/rider-hour at ≥ 1,050 orders a day (or a fee losing ≤ 15% of volume); CAC repaid within 12 months; ring-fenced funding

Four board decisions: decline launch and pop-up extension (Board, Jan 2027); approve $0.8M hires in two tranches (CEO, Q1); build store-based offer (CTO/Sales, Q2); adopt triggers and runway reporting (CFO, Q1)
April 2027 checkpoint: late-stage conversions, pilot interest, ARR growth against 34%, first trigger dashboard; hold tranche 2 if growth is below 34%
Store-based fast delivery for pipeline grocers gives Parcelbird a share of the market's growth
Per-order calculation table for pop-up, median, best observed and plan
Seven judgement calls where the pack is ambiguous; only the software cost base is optimistic for C
